title: How Much Do Real Estate Wholesalers Make Per Deal? (Real Numbers Inside)
excerpt: Curious how much real estate wholesalers make per deal? This guide breaks down average fees, real examples, and what separates a $3,000 deal from a $30,000 payday.

sections.content: If you're new to wholesaling, the first question on your mind is probably: how much do real estate wholesalers make per deal? The honest answer is — it varies a lot. Some wholesalers pocket $3,000 on a starter deal. Others walk away with $25,000 or more on a single transaction. What drives that difference comes down to your market, your negotiation skills, and how well you understand the numbers. If you're just getting started, check out the [Wholesale Real Estate for Beginners: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesale-real-estate-beginners-guide) before diving deep into the income side of things. But if you're ready to talk dollars and cents, let's break it all down.
What Is a Wholesale Assignment Fee?

When a wholesaler finds a distressed property, they put it under contract at a below-market price and then sell that contract to an investor for more than they paid. The difference between those two numbers is called the assignment fee — and that's how wholesalers get paid. If you're not totally clear on the mechanics yet, read [What Is Wholesale Real Estate? A Simple Explanation](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/what-is-wholesale-real-estate-simple-explanation) first. There are no mortgages, no renovation costs, and no months of holding expenses. You're essentially selling your right to buy the property, not the property itself.
Average Wholesale Fee: What the Numbers Look Like

The national average wholesale assignment fee falls somewhere between $5,000 and $15,000 per deal. That said, the range is wide. Entry-level wholesalers in smaller markets often start around $3,000 to $5,000. Experienced wholesalers in competitive metros regularly earn $15,000 to $30,000 or more per assignment. In some high-value markets — think coastal cities or luxury segments — a single deal can hit $50,000+. The fee isn't random. It's calculated based on the After Repair Value (ARV) of the property, the estimated rehab costs, and how much room you can build into the deal for both yourself and the end buyer investor.
The Formula Wholesalers Use

Most wholesalers use a variation of the 70% rule to find their maximum allowable offer (MAO). Here's how it works: MAO = (ARV × 70%) − Estimated Repairs − Your Assignment Fee. Let's say a home has an ARV of $200,000 and needs $30,000 in repairs. The investor's max buy price is roughly $110,000 (200,000 × 0.70 − 30,000). If you get the property under contract at $95,000, you have a $15,000 spread to work with. That $15,000 is your assignment fee. Use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run these numbers fast before locking in any contract.

Always verify your ARV with at least 3 comparable sales (comps) within a one-mile radius and sold within the last 90 days. A wrong ARV estimate is the #1 reason wholesalers lose deals or leave money on the table.
Real-World Examples by Market
Your geography matters more than almost anything else when it comes to wholesale fees. Here are three realistic examples from active wholesaling markets:

items: Atlanta, GA: A wholesaler finds a 3/2 ranch home with an ARV of $185,000 needing $35,000 in work. They get it under contract at $80,000 and assign it to a flipper for $93,000 — a $13,000 assignment fee. Explore active deals in [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga).

Houston, TX: A distressed duplex has an ARV of $280,000 and needs $45,000 in repairs. The wholesaler contracts it at $120,000 and assigns at $138,000 — an $18,000 fee. See what's moving in [Houston](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/houston-tx).

Phoenix, AZ: A fire-damaged home with an ARV of $350,000 needs $60,000 in work. The wholesaler locks it up at $160,000 and assigns at $183,000 — a $23,000 payday on a single deal. Check the [Phoenix market](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) for current opportunities.

sections.content: How Many Deals Do Wholesalers Close Per Month?

Volume matters just as much as per-deal income. A part-time wholesaler might close 1 to 2 deals per month, bringing in $5,000 to $20,000. A full-time wholesaler with a small team and solid systems can close 4 to 10 deals per month. At an average of $10,000 per deal, that's $40,000 to $100,000 monthly gross income — before marketing and overhead costs. It sounds impressive, but don't overlook expenses. Direct mail campaigns, skip tracing software, driving for dollars apps, and CRM tools can cost $1,500 to $5,000 per month depending on your scale. Net profit margins typically run 50% to 70% for established wholesalers.

'Your first deal will likely be your hardest and your smallest. Most successful wholesalers close a $4,000 deal before they ever close a $40,000 one. Don't skip the learning curve — every deal teaches you something the last one didn't.' — Common wisdom among experienced real estate wholesalers
What Separates a $3,000 Deal from a $30,000 Deal?

It's easy to assume bigger fees come from more expensive homes. That's partially true, but the real difference often comes down to negotiation and lead quality. Wholesalers who build strong seller relationships — especially with motivated sellers facing foreclosure, divorce, probate, or major repairs — consistently negotiate deeper discounts. Deeper discounts mean bigger spreads. Wholesalers who rely only on low-effort methods like cold calling random lists tend to find shallower deals. The other factor is your buyer's list. If you have 50 active cash buyers ready to move fast, you can command a higher fee because you're delivering certainty and speed. If you're scrambling to find a buyer after you get a contract, investors will sense the pressure and negotiate your fee down.
Legal Considerations That Affect Your Earnings

Before you start calculating paydays, make sure you understand the legal side. Some states have specific rules about how wholesalers can market and assign contracts. A few states require a real estate license for certain wholesaling activities. Assignment fees above a certain threshold can also raise questions if your contract language isn't tight. Read the [Is Wholesale Real Estate Legal? State-by-State Guide 2026](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/is-wholesale-real-estate-legal-state-guide) to make sure you're operating correctly in your market. Your fees don't count for much if you're doing business the wrong way.

Always use a properly written wholesale contract with an assignment clause built in. A poorly written contract can cost you the deal entirely. Download a ready-to-use template from [How to Get a Wholesale Real Estate Contract (Free Template)](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-real-estate-contract-template).
How to Increase Your Assignment Fee on Every Deal

items: Negotiate harder on the buy side: Every dollar you shave off the contract price is a dollar added to your assignment fee.
Target higher-value neighborhoods: A 10% spread on a $400,000 ARV property is worth far more than the same spread on a $100,000 home.
Build a strong cash buyer list: Buyers who trust you and close fast will pay more for that reliability.
Use accurate ARV data: Overestimating ARV kills deals. Underestimating leaves your fee on the table.
Double close on large fees: If your assignment fee is $20,000 or more, some buyers get uncomfortable seeing the spread. A double close hides this and protects your position.
Do deals in growing markets: Active markets like Atlanta, Houston, and Phoenix generate more motivated sellers and more active buyers — which means more room for fees.
